rationale: The entry’s distinguishing claim is not that Egypt generally means bondage, but that Revelation 11:8 applies that symbol specifically to Jerusalem. The locative clause “where also our Lord was crucified” most naturally identifies the great city as Jerusalem; Galatians 4:25 independently calls contemporary Jerusalem a city “in bondage”; Isaiah 1:10 demonstrates the prophetic practice of assigning a corrupt covenant city another wicked city’s name; and Matthew 23:37 supports the charge of covenant corruption. The broader counter-reading of an abstract anti-God world-city preserves Egypt’s oppression theme but explains the Jerusalem-specific locative and intertextual details less directly.
book_core_identification: In Revelation 11:8, the city spiritually called Egypt is Jerusalem, portrayed as being in bondage.
book_secondary_elaborations: Its bondage is bondage under worldly rule.
Its designation as Egypt reflects covenant corruption.
chapter_only_objections: The chapter’s further identification of Babylon the Great and the woman of Revelation 17–18 with Jerusalem requires additional arguments beyond the glossary entry.
The chapter’s extensive scene-by-scene Exodus correspondences and its interpretation of Aaron’s rod, the serpent, and Babylon are not established merely by the texts supporting this entry.
strongest_counter_interpretation: Revelation 11:8’s “great city” is the universal anti-God world-city, commonly associated with Rome or eschatological Babylon. It is spiritually called Egypt because it oppresses God’s people, while “where also our Lord was crucified” characterizes the world’s collective hostility to Christ rather than geographically identifying Jerusalem.
counter_core_identification: Spiritual Egypt is the transhistorical anti-God world-city or imperial order, not Jerusalem specifically.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that Revelation 11:8 identifies spiritual Egypt specifically with Jerusalem.
counter_case: Egypt conventionally symbolizes oppression and bondage, which readily characterizes a hostile imperial world-system.
Revelation’s repeated use of “the great city” for Babylon can favor reading Revelation 11:8 within the book’s broader Babylon imagery.
A theological reading of Christ as rejected by the world can make “where also our Lord was crucified” symbolic rather than geographical.
book_explanatory_advantages: It takes “where also our Lord was crucified” in its straightforward locative sense and supplies the uniquely recognizable city: Jerusalem.
Galatians 4:25 provides an unusually close independent equation: present Jerusalem is “in bondage,” precisely the feature represented by Egypt.
Isaiah 1:10 supplies an Old Testament precedent for spiritually renaming corrupt Jerusalem after a notoriously wicked city.
Matthew 23:37 directly associates Jerusalem with killing God’s messengers, supporting the entry’s covenant-corruption description.
The interpretation explains why Revelation uses both Sodom and Egypt as spiritual names while retaining a concrete city referent.
counter_explanatory_advantages: It aligns the Egypt symbol with the dominant Christian typology of oppression and worldly bondage.
It can integrate Revelation 11:8 with readings in which “the great city” consistently denotes Babylon, Rome, or a worldwide anti-God order.
unresolved_objections: Revelation’s broader use of “the great city” leaves some room for a transhistorical or typological referent extending beyond historical Jerusalem.
“Under worldly rule” is inferential rather than stated verbatim in the supplied excerpts, though it coheres with Jerusalem’s stated bondage and historical setting.
